about: Chapter 2, Fractions: 63 patterns, three or four for each of the 15 skills (1 and 2 marks), three 3-mark and three 5-mark written questions, and three 4-mark case studies, drawn from the chapter's 500 questions. All DRAFT until Ashalatha approves them.

patterns.text: A {obj} is cut into {n} equal parts. What fraction of the whole {obj} is one part?

wrong.mistake: writes the number of parts as the fraction
counts the parts that are not taken
counts the cuts (or the cuts and both ends) instead of the equal parts

patterns.hint: The denominator tells how many equal parts make the whole.
patterns.explanation: The whole {obj} has {n} equal parts, so one part is 1/{n} of it.
patterns.misconception: Treats unequal pieces as valid fractional parts or compares pieces from different-sized wholes directly.
patterns.notes: 12 everyday things (roti, paratha, chikki bar, ribbon...); 3 to 16 equal parts.

patterns.text: Each piece is 1/{n} of a {obj}, and all the {obj}s are the same size. How many such pieces make {w} whole {obj}{'' if w == 1 else 's'}?
patterns.hint: 1/{n} means {n} equal pieces make one whole.
patterns.explanation: {n} pieces of 1/{n} make one whole {obj}, so {w} whole {obj}{'' if w == 1 else 's'} need {n} × {w} = {n * w} pieces.
patterns.misconception: Treats unequal pieces as valid fractional parts or compares pieces from different-sized wholes directly.
patterns.notes: 2 to 20 pieces in a whole; usually one whole, sometimes 2 or 3 wholes of the same size.

choice.right: Yes, because all the parts are equal
choice.w1: No, because the parts must be coloured first
choice.w2: No, because there are too many parts
choice.w3: Only if the parts have different shapes

choice.right: No, because the parts are not equal
choice.w1: Yes, because there are that many pieces
choice.w2: Yes, if the largest piece is chosen
choice.w3: Yes, because all the pieces come from one whole

patterns.text: {who.name} cuts a {obj} into {n} pieces that are {c.desc}. Can one piece be called 1/{n} of the {obj}?

wrong.mistake: adds a condition that has nothing to do with equal parts
judges by the number of pieces instead of whether they are equal
forgets that the parts of a fraction must be equal

patterns.hint: A fraction like 1/{n} needs {n} equal parts of one whole.
patterns.explanation: 1/{n} means one of {n} equal parts of the same whole. Here the pieces are {c.desc}, so the answer is: {c.right}.
patterns.misconception: Treats unequal pieces as valid fractional parts or compares pieces from different-sized wholes directly.
patterns.notes: 3 to 10 pieces; the pieces are equal or of different sizes, so the answer is sometimes Yes and sometimes No.

patterns.text: A ribbon {s * n} cm long and another ribbon {t * n} cm long are each cut into {n} equal pieces. One piece of each is called 1/{n} of its ribbon. How many centimetres longer is the piece from the longer ribbon?

steps.text: Finds each piece: {s * n} ÷ {n} = {s} cm and {t * n} ÷ {n} = {t} cm.
Finds the difference: {t} − {s} = {t - s} cm. (Both pieces are 1/{n}, but of different wholes.)

patterns.hint: 1/{n} of a longer ribbon is a longer piece. Find each piece first.
patterns.explanation: {s * n} ÷ {n} = {s} cm and {t * n} ÷ {n} = {t} cm. The pieces have the same fraction name but different wholes, so they differ by {t} − {s} = {t - s} cm.
patterns.misconception: Treats unequal pieces as valid fractional parts or compares pieces from different-sized wholes directly.
patterns.notes: 2 to 6 pieces each; pieces of the shorter ribbon 4 to 12 cm, of the longer 2 to 10 cm more; lengths are whole multiples.

patterns.text: What is the {part.w} of the fraction {a}/{b}?
patterns.hint: The numerator is the top number; the denominator, below the line, tells how many equal parts make the whole.
patterns.explanation: In {a}/{b}, the numerator is {a} and the denominator is {b}. So the {part.w} is {a if part.top == 1 else b}.
patterns.misconception: Interchanges numerator and denominator or counts unselected parts as the numerator.
patterns.notes: Proper fractions in simplest form with denominators 3 to 20; asks for the numerator or the denominator.

patterns.text: A {set.whole} has {n} equal {set.thing}, and {s} of them {'is' if s == 1 else 'are'} {set.col}. What fraction of the {set.whole} is {set.col}? Write it as a/b.
patterns.hint: The numerator counts the {set.col} {set.thing}; the denominator counts all the equal {set.thing}.
patterns.explanation: {s} of the {n} equal {set.thing} are {set.col}, so the fraction is {s}/{n}.
patterns.misconception: Interchanges numerator and denominator or counts unselected parts as the numerator.
patterns.notes: 4 to 16 equal parts; the count chosen shares no factor with the total, so the fraction is already in simplest form.

patterns.text: A {set.whole} has {n} equal {set.thing}. {s} of them {'is' if s == 1 else 'are'} {set.col}. What fraction of the {set.whole} is NOT {set.col}? Write it as a/b.
patterns.hint: First count the {set.thing} that are not {set.col}.
patterns.explanation: {n} − {s} = {n - s} of the {set.thing} {'is' if n - s == 1 else 'are'} not {set.col}, so the fraction is {n - s}/{n}.
patterns.misconception: Interchanges numerator and denominator or counts unselected parts as the numerator.
patterns.notes: 5 to 18 equal parts; the answer is in simplest form and differs from the fraction that IS coloured (a trap for counting the wrong parts).

patterns.text: A school garden has {n} equal beds. {x} beds have marigolds and {y} beds have roses. The other beds are empty. What fraction of the beds are empty? Write it as a/b.

steps.text: Counts the empty beds: {n} − {x} − {y} = {e}.
Writes the fraction with the whole garden as the denominator: {e}/{n}.

patterns.hint: Find how many beds are empty, then compare with all {n} beds.
patterns.explanation: Empty beds = {n} − {x} − {y} = {e}. There are {n} equal beds in all, so {e}/{n} of the beds are empty.
patterns.misconception: Interchanges numerator and denominator or counts unselected parts as the numerator.
patterns.notes: 8 to 20 beds; marigolds and roses each up to a third of the beds; the empty fraction is in simplest form.

patterns.text: Two {obj}s are the same size. One is cut into {a} equal pieces and the other into {b} equal pieces. Which piece is larger?

wrong.mistake: thinks a larger denominator makes a larger piece
thinks every piece of a same-sized whole is the same
doesn't use the number of equal pieces to judge size

patterns.hint: The more equal pieces a whole is cut into, the smaller each piece.
patterns.explanation: The same {obj} shared into {a} pieces gives bigger pieces than shared into {b}. So 1/{a} is larger than 1/{b}.
patterns.misconception: Assumes a larger denominator means a larger unit-fraction piece.
patterns.notes: Two same-sized wholes cut into 2 to 12 and up to 20 pieces; the options show 1/a, 1/b and two others.

patterns.text: How many 1/{n} pieces make {w} whole{'' if w == 1 else 's'}?
patterns.hint: {n} pieces of 1/{n} make one whole.
patterns.explanation: One whole is {n} pieces of 1/{n}, so {w} whole{'' if w == 1 else 's'} need {n} × {w} = {n * w} pieces.
patterns.misconception: Assumes a larger denominator means a larger unit-fraction piece.
patterns.notes: Unit fractions 1/2 to 1/15; one, two or three wholes.

patterns.text: Order these unit fractions from greatest to least: 1/{x}, 1/{y}, 1/{z}. Enter greatest;middle;least.

steps.text: Uses the idea that a smaller denominator means a larger piece (1/{lo} is the greatest).
Gives the full order: 1/{lo}, 1/{mid}, 1/{hi}.

patterns.hint: With 1 as the numerator, the fraction with the smallest denominator is the greatest.
patterns.explanation: The fewer the equal pieces, the bigger each one: 1/{lo} > 1/{mid} > 1/{hi}.
patterns.misconception: Assumes a larger denominator means a larger unit-fraction piece.
patterns.notes: Three different unit fractions 1/2 to 1/15, never already listed in the order of their denominators.

patterns.text: {p.name} gets 1/{a} of a {obj}. {q.name} gets 1/{b} of another {obj} of the same size. Who gets more?

options.correct: p.name if a < b else q.name

wrong.expr: q.name if a < b else p.name
wrong.mistake: picks the share with the larger denominator
thinks unit fractions of the same whole are all equal

wrong.expr: 'It depends on how the pieces are cut'
wrong.mistake: forgets that the parts are equal parts of the same-sized whole

patterns.hint: Compare the denominators: fewer equal pieces means bigger pieces.
patterns.explanation: 1/{min(a, b)} is larger than 1/{max(a, b)} of the same-sized {obj}, so {p.name if a < b else q.name} gets more.
patterns.misconception: Assumes a larger denominator means a larger unit-fraction piece.
patterns.notes: Two different children; unit fractions 1/2 to 1/12 of same-sized wholes.

patterns.text: {who.name} has {t} {g.many}. {who.name} gives away {a}/{b} of them. How many {g.many} does {who.name} give away?
patterns.hint: First find 1/{b} of {t} by dividing by {b}.
patterns.explanation: 1/{b} of {t} is {t} ÷ {b} = {k}. So {a}/{b} of {t} is {k} × {a} = {a * k}.
patterns.misconception: Multiplies by the denominator instead of dividing the whole into equal groups first.
patterns.notes: Fractions with denominators 2 to 12 in simplest form; the total is a multiple of the denominator, at most 120.

patterns.text: {a}/{b} of the {g.many} in a box is {a * k} {g.many}. How many {g.many} are in the whole box?

steps.text: Finds 1/{b}: {a * k} ÷ {a} = {k}.
Finds the whole: {k} × {b} = {b * k}.

patterns.hint: {a}/{b} is {a} equal groups out of {b}. Find one group first.
patterns.explanation: {a} {'group' if (a) == 1 else 'groups'} make {a * k}, so one group is {a * k} ÷ {a} = {k}. The whole box has {b} {'group' if (b) == 1 else 'groups'}: {k} × {b} = {b * k}.
patterns.misconception: Multiplies by the denominator instead of dividing the whole into equal groups first.
patterns.notes: Denominators 3 to 10; the part given is a whole number of equal groups of 2 to 12.

patterns.text: {s} of {t} {g.many} are {col}. What fraction of the {g.many} are {col}? Write it in simplest form.
patterns.hint: Write {s}/{t}, then divide the numerator and denominator by the same number.
patterns.explanation: {s}/{t} = {s // gcd(s, t)}/{t // gcd(s, t)} after dividing both by {gcd(s, t)}.
patterns.misconception: Multiplies by the denominator instead of dividing the whole into equal groups first.
patterns.notes: 6 to 40 things; the fraction always simplifies (and not to 1 over something, so it isn't trivial).

patterns.text: Out of ₹{t:num} saved, {a}/{b} is spent on {what}. How much money is spent on {what}?

wrong.mistake: finds one equal share and stops
finds the money left instead of the money spent
takes one equal share too few

patterns.hint: Find 1/{b} of ₹{t:num} first, then take {a} of those shares.
patterns.explanation: 1/{b} of ₹{t:num} is ₹{k}. So {a}/{b} is {a} × ₹{k} = ₹{a * k}.
patterns.misconception: Multiplies by the denominator instead of dividing the whole into equal groups first.
patterns.notes: Denominators 3 to 10; amounts are the denominator times 5 to 50 (in fives). Wrong options: one share, one share too few, the money left (so the right answer is sometimes the largest option, sometimes not).

patterns.text: A {obj} is made of {n} equal pieces, each 1/{n} of it. {k} {'piece is' if k == 1 else 'pieces are'} already in place. How many more pieces complete the whole?
patterns.hint: The whole needs {n} pieces of 1/{n}.
patterns.explanation: {n} pieces make the whole and {k} are in place, so {n} − {k} = {n - k} more are needed.
patterns.misconception: Changes the denominator when combining equal-sized pieces.
patterns.notes: 4 to 16 pieces in the whole.

patterns.text: {a}/{n} of a {job.what} is {job.done}. What fraction of the {job.what} is still left? Write it as a/b.
patterns.hint: One whole is {n}/{n}.
patterns.explanation: The whole is {n}/{n}. {n}/{n} − {a}/{n} = {n - a}/{n} is still left.
patterns.misconception: Changes the denominator when combining equal-sized pieces.
patterns.notes: Denominators 5 to 16; the part left is in simplest form.

patterns.text: A {obj} is cut into {n} equal pieces. {p.name} eats {a}/{n} of it and {q.name} eats {b}/{n} of it. What fraction of the {obj} is left? Write it as a/b.
patterns.hint: The pieces are all 1/{n}, so the denominator stays {n}.
patterns.misconception: Changes the denominator when combining equal-sized pieces.
patterns.notes: 5 to 12 equal pieces; at least one piece is left; the answer is in simplest form.

patterns.text: {who.name} is making one whole with pieces of 1/{n}. {who.name} puts down {a} pieces, then {b} more. How many more pieces are needed, and what fraction of the whole is still missing? Enter pieces;fraction missing.

steps.text: Pieces still needed: {n} − {a} − {b} = {n - a - b}.
Missing fraction: {n - a - b}/{n} (the denominator stays {n}).

patterns.hint: One whole is {n} pieces of 1/{n}.
patterns.explanation: {a} + {b} = {a + b} pieces are down, so {n} − {a + b} = {n - a - b} more are needed. They make {n - a - b}/{n} of the whole.
patterns.misconception: Changes the denominator when combining equal-sized pieces.
patterns.notes: 6 to 15 pieces in the whole; the missing fraction is in simplest form.

values.name: c
values.expr: a * k if mode != 'add' else a + k

values.name: d
values.expr: b * k if mode == 'eq' else (b + k if mode == 'add' else b * k + 1)

patterns.text: Are {a}/{b} and {c}/{d} equivalent fractions?

options.correct: 'Yes, they show the same part of a whole' if mode == 'eq' else 'No, they show different amounts'

wrong.expr: 'No, they show different amounts' if mode == 'eq' else 'Yes, they show the same part of a whole'
wrong.mistake: checks the numbers' size instead of one scale factor
brings in different wholes, which has nothing to do with it

wrong.expr: 'It cannot be checked without a picture'
wrong.mistake: doesn't know how to check with a scale factor

patterns.hint: Equivalent fractions come from multiplying the numerator AND denominator by the same number.
patterns.explanation: {a} × {k} = {a * k} and {b} × {k} = {b * k}, so {a}/{b} = {a * k}/{b * k}. The fraction {c}/{d} {'is' if mode == 'eq' else 'is not'} {a * k}/{b * k}, so the answer is {'Yes' if mode == 'eq' else 'No'}.
patterns.misconception: Changes only the numerator or only the denominator and calls the result equivalent.
patterns.notes: Fractions with denominators 3 to 9, scale factor 2 to 5. Half the time equivalent; otherwise the same number was added to both terms, or only the numerator was scaled with the denominator one more.

patterns.text: Which fraction is equivalent to {f.q}?

wrong.mistake: adds the same number to the numerator and denominator
multiplies only the denominator
multiplies only the numerator

patterns.hint: Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the same number.
patterns.explanation: Multiplying both terms of {f.q} by {f.k} gives {f.r}, so {f.r} is equivalent to {f.q}.
patterns.misconception: Changes only the numerator or only the denominator and calls the result equivalent.
patterns.notes: 60 fractions in simplest form with denominators 3 to 10 and scale factors 2 to 5 (listed in the pattern). Wrong options: the same number added to both terms, only the denominator scaled, only the numerator scaled.

choice.right: No, adding the same number does not keep the fraction equal
Yes, multiplying both terms by the same number keeps it equal

values.name: c
values.expr: a + k if how.c == 'plus' else a * k

values.name: d
values.expr: b + k if how.c == 'plus' else b * k

patterns.text: {who.name} changed {a}/{b} to {c}/{d} by {'adding ' if how.c == 'plus' else 'multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by '}{k}{' to both the numerator and the denominator' if how.c == 'plus' else ''}. {who.name} says {c}/{d} is equivalent to {a}/{b}. Is that right?

wrong.expr: 'Yes, adding the same number keeps the fraction equal' if how.c == 'plus' else 'No, multiplying changes the size of the fraction'
wrong.mistake: uses the wrong rule for making equivalent fractions

wrong.expr: 'Yes, because both fractions are less than one'
wrong.mistake: decides by a property both fractions share instead of their value

wrong.expr: 'No, equivalent fractions must have the same denominator'
wrong.mistake: thinks equivalent fractions need the same denominator

steps.text: Checks with one scale factor: {a}/{b} = {a * k}/{b * k} (both terms × {k}), and {c}/{d} {'is' if how.c == 'times' else 'is not'} that fraction.
Concludes correctly: {how.right}.

patterns.hint: Equivalent fractions come from multiplying (or dividing) both terms by the same number.
patterns.explanation: {a}/{b} = {a * k}/{b * k} (both terms × {k}). {who.name} got {c}/{d}, so: {how.right}.
patterns.misconception: Changes only the numerator or only the denominator and calls the result equivalent.
patterns.notes: Fractions with denominators 3 to 9; 2 to 4 is added to both terms, or both terms are multiplied by it (so the answer is sometimes No, sometimes Yes).

patterns.text: Complete the equivalent fraction: {a}/{b} = ___/{b * k}.
patterns.hint: What was {b} multiplied by to get {b * k}? Multiply {a} by the same number.
patterns.explanation: {b} × {k} = {b * k}, so the numerator is {a} × {k} = {a * k}: {a}/{b} = {a * k}/{b * k}.
patterns.misconception: Adds the same number to numerator and denominator instead of multiplying both by one scale factor.
patterns.notes: Fractions in simplest form with denominators 2 to 13; the new denominator is 2 to 6 times bigger.

patterns.text: Complete the equivalent fraction: {a}/{b} = {a * k}/___.
patterns.hint: {a} was multiplied by {k}. Multiply the denominator by {k} too.
patterns.explanation: {a} × {k} = {a * k}, so the denominator is {b} × {k} = {b * k}.
patterns.misconception: Adds the same number to numerator and denominator instead of multiplying both by one scale factor.
patterns.notes: Denominators 3 to 12; scale factor 2 to 5.

patterns.text: Find the two missing numbers: {a}/{b} = {a * k}/___ = ___/{b * m}. Enter first;second.

steps.text: First missing number: {a} × {k} = {a * k}, so the denominator is {b} × {k} = {b * k}.
Second missing number: {b} × {m} = {b * m}, so the numerator is {a} × {m} = {a * m}.

patterns.hint: Each fraction is {a}/{b} with both terms multiplied by the same number.
patterns.misconception: Adds the same number to numerator and denominator instead of multiplying both by one scale factor.
patterns.notes: Denominators 2 to 9; two different scale factors (2 to 5 and 2 to 6).

patterns.text: Choose the correct symbol: {x}/{d} ___ {y}/{d}.

wrong.mistake: reverses the order of the numerators
thinks the fractions are equal because they share a number
thinks the fractions can't be compared without a picture

patterns.hint: The denominators are the same, so compare the numerators.
patterns.explanation: Both fractions count pieces of size 1/{d}. {x} {'piece' if x == 1 else 'pieces'} {'<' if x < y else '>'} {y} {'piece' if y == 1 else 'pieces'}, so {x}/{d} {'<' if x < y else '>'} {y}/{d}.
patterns.misconception: Compares denominators even when they are already equal.
patterns.notes: Denominators 3 to 20; two different numerators below the denominator.

patterns.text: Order from least to greatest: {x}/{d}, {y}/{d}, {z}/{d}. Enter least;middle;greatest.
patterns.hint: Same denominator: the fraction with the smallest numerator is the least.
patterns.explanation: All three are counted in pieces of 1/{d}, so order the numerators: {lo} < {mid} < {hi}. The order is {lo}/{d}, {mid}/{d}, {hi}/{d}.
patterns.misconception: Compares denominators even when they are already equal.
patterns.notes: Three fractions with the same denominator (5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 or 13), each in simplest form, never already in order.

patterns.text: Two {obj}s of the same size are each cut into {d} equal pieces. {p.name} eats {x}/{d} of one and {q.name} eats {y}/{d} of the other. Who eats more?

options.correct: p.name if x > y else q.name

wrong.expr: q.name if x > y else p.name
wrong.mistake: reverses the comparison of the numerators
sees the same denominator and thinks the amounts are equal
doesn't compare the numerators when the denominators match

patterns.hint: The pieces are the same size, so count the pieces.
patterns.explanation: Both ate pieces of 1/{d}. {max(x, y)} pieces is more than {min(x, y)}, so {p.name if x > y else q.name} eats more.
patterns.misconception: Compares denominators even when they are already equal.
patterns.notes: 4 to 12 equal pieces; two different children and amounts.

patterns.text: Choose the correct symbol: {n}/{a} ___ {n}/{b}.

wrong.mistake: chooses the fraction with the larger denominator as greater
thinks the fractions are equal because they share a number
thinks the fractions can't be compared without a picture

patterns.hint: The numerators are the same. Which has bigger pieces?
patterns.explanation: Both have {n} {'piece' if n == 1 else 'pieces'}. Pieces of 1/{min(a, b)} are bigger than pieces of 1/{max(a, b)}, so {n}/{a} {'<' if b < a else '>'} {n}/{b}.
patterns.misconception: Chooses the fraction with the larger denominator as greater.
patterns.notes: Same numerator 1 to 11; two different denominators above it, up to 20.

patterns.text: Order from least to greatest: {n}/{x}, {n}/{y}, {n}/{z}. Enter least;middle;greatest.

steps.text: Uses the idea that with the same numerator, the larger denominator gives the smaller fraction ({n}/{hi} is the least).
Gives the full order: {n}/{hi}, {n}/{mid}, {n}/{lo}.

patterns.hint: Same numerator: more pieces in the whole means each piece is smaller.
patterns.explanation: Each fraction has {n} {'piece' if n == 1 else 'pieces'}; the larger the denominator, the smaller the pieces. So {n}/{hi} < {n}/{mid} < {n}/{lo}.
patterns.misconception: Chooses the fraction with the larger denominator as greater.
patterns.notes: Same numerator 1 to 7; three different denominators up to 16, each fraction in simplest form, never already in order.

patterns.text: Two identical {c.many}, P and Q, hold some {c.what}. P is {n}/{a} full and Q is {n}/{b} full. Which has more {c.what} in it?

wrong.mistake: chooses the fraction with the larger denominator
sees the same numerator and thinks the amounts are equal

wrong.expr: 'It depends on the size of the containers'
wrong.mistake: forgets the containers are identical

patterns.hint: Same numerator: compare the size of the parts.
patterns.explanation: 1/{min(a, b)} of the container is bigger than 1/{max(a, b)}, so {n}/{min(a, b)} is more. {'P' if a < b else 'Q'} has more.
patterns.misconception: Chooses the fraction with the larger denominator as greater.
patterns.notes: Same numerator 1 to 5; denominators up to 12.

int.min: 1 if rel == 'lt' else (d if rel == 'eq' else d + 1)
int.max: d - 1 if rel == 'lt' else (d if rel == 'eq' else 2 * d - 1)

values.name: c
values.expr: 'Less than 1' if n < d else ('Equal to 1' if n == d else 'Greater than 1')

patterns.text: Is {n}/{d} less than 1, equal to 1 or greater than 1?

wrong.expr: 'Equal to 1' if c == 'Less than 1' else 'Less than 1'
wrong.mistake: doesn't compare the numerator with the denominator

wrong.expr: 'Greater than 1' if c != 'Greater than 1' else 'Equal to 1'
wrong.mistake: doesn't compare the numerator with the denominator

wrong.expr: 'It cannot be told without a picture'
wrong.mistake: thinks a fraction can't be compared with one from its numbers

patterns.hint: One whole is {d}/{d}. Compare {n} with {d}.
patterns.explanation: One whole is {d}/{d}. {n} is {'less than' if n < d else ('equal to' if n == d else 'greater than')} {d}, so {n}/{d} is {'less than' if n < d else ('equal to' if n == d else 'greater than')} 1.
patterns.misconception: Assumes every fraction is less than one regardless of its numerator.
patterns.notes: Denominators 2 to 15; the numerator is below, equal to or above the denominator (less than 2 wholes).

require: n3 > n1 or d3 > d1 or n4 > n1
patterns.text: Which of these fractions is greater than 1?

wrong.mistake: thinks a fraction close to its denominator is more than one
looks at the size of the numbers, not the numerator against the denominator
looks at the size of the numbers, not the numerator against the denominator

patterns.hint: A fraction is greater than 1 when its numerator is greater than its denominator.
patterns.explanation: In {n1}/{d1}, the numerator {n1} is greater than the denominator {d1}, so it is more than one whole. The others have a numerator smaller than the denominator.
patterns.misconception: Assumes every fraction is less than one regardless of its numerator.
patterns.notes: One improper fraction (less than 2) and three proper fractions with denominators up to 12, all in simplest form; at least one wrong option uses bigger numbers than the right one.

values.name: k
values.expr: (0 if big == 1 else 2) if says.g == 1 else (1 if big == 0 else 3)

patterns.text: {who.name} says, “{n}/{d} is {says.w} than 1.” Is {who.name} right?

options.correct: 'Yes, the numerator is greater than the denominator' if (k) % 4 == 0 else ('Yes, the numerator is less than the denominator' if (k) % 4 == 1 else ('No, the numerator is less than the denominator' if (k) % 4 == 2 else 'No, the numerator is greater than the denominator'))

wrong.expr: 'Yes, the numerator is greater than the denominator' if (k + 1) % 4 == 0 else ('Yes, the numerator is less than the denominator' if (k + 1) % 4 == 1 else ('No, the numerator is less than the denominator' if (k + 1) % 4 == 2 else 'No, the numerator is greater than the denominator'))
wrong.mistake: doesn't compare the numerator with the denominator

steps.text: Compares {n} with {d}: {n}/{d} is {'greater' if n > d else 'less'} than {d}/{d} = 1.

patterns.explanation: One whole is {d}/{d}. {n} is {'greater' if n > d else 'less'} than {d}, so {n}/{d} is {'greater' if n > d else 'less'} than 1, and {who.name} is {'right' if (n > d) == (says.g == 1) else 'not right'}.
patterns.misconception: Assumes every fraction is less than one regardless of its numerator.
patterns.notes: Proper or improper fractions (below 2) with denominators 3 to 12; the child claims 'greater than 1' or 'less than 1', so the right answer is any of four (Yes or No, numerator bigger or smaller).

patterns.text: Write {n}/{d} as a mixed number: ___ wholes and ___/{d}. Enter whole number;numerator.
patterns.hint: How many groups of {d} are in {n}? The pieces left over stay over {d}.
patterns.explanation: {n} ÷ {d} = {w} remainder {r}, so {n}/{d} = {w} {r}/{d}.
patterns.misconception: Uses the remainder as a whole-number part or changes the denominator during conversion.
patterns.notes: Denominators 2 to 12; 1 to 5 wholes; the fraction part is in simplest form.

patterns.text: Write {w} {r}/{d} as an improper fraction: {w} {r}/{d} = ___/{d}. What is the missing numerator?
patterns.hint: Each whole is {d}/{d}. Multiply {w} by {d}, then add {r}.
patterns.explanation: {w} {'whole' if w == 1 else 'wholes'} = {w} × {d} = {w * d} pieces of 1/{d}. Add {r}: {w * d} + {r} = {w * d + r}, so {w} {r}/{d} = {w * d + r}/{d}.
patterns.misconception: Uses the remainder as a whole-number part or changes the denominator during conversion.
patterns.notes: Denominators 2 to 12; 1 to 5 wholes. Asked as the missing numerator, so the denominator is given.

patterns.text: How many complete wholes are in {w * d + r}/{d}?
patterns.hint: Count the complete groups of {d} in {w * d + r}.
patterns.explanation: {w * d + r} ÷ {d} = {w} remainder {r}, so there are {w} complete wholes.
patterns.misconception: Uses the remainder as a whole-number part or changes the denominator during conversion.
patterns.notes: Denominators 2 to 12; 1 to 8 wholes with some left over.

patterns.text: Each {item.one} is cut into {d} equal pieces. {who.name} has {n} such pieces. How many whole {item.one}s can be made from them, and how many pieces are left over? Enter wholes;pieces left.

steps.text: Divides: {n} ÷ {d} = {w} remainder {r} (or {n}/{d} = {w} {r}/{d}).
Answers {w} whole {item.one}s and {r} {'piece' if r == 1 else 'pieces'} left over.

patterns.hint: {d} pieces make one whole {item.one}.
patterns.explanation: {n} ÷ {d} = {w} remainder {r}, so {n}/{d} = {w} {r}/{d}: {w} whole {item.one}s and {r} {'piece' if r == 1 else 'pieces'} left.
patterns.misconception: Uses the remainder as a whole-number part or changes the denominator during conversion.
patterns.notes: 3 to 8 pieces in each whole; 2 to 6 wholes and some pieces left over.

patterns.text: A number line from 0 to 1 is divided into {d} equal parts. Counting the marks after 0, what fraction is at mark number {k}? Write it as a/b.
patterns.hint: Each part is 1/{d}. Count the parts from 0.
patterns.explanation: Each part is 1/{d}. Mark number {k} is {k} {'part' if k == 1 else 'parts'} from 0, so it shows {k}/{d}.
patterns.misconception: Counts tick marks instead of intervals or starts the numerator count at one rather than zero.
patterns.notes: Lines split into 3 to 12 equal parts; the fraction is in simplest form.

patterns.text: A number line from 0 to 1 has {d} equal parts. Counting the marks after 0, which mark number shows {k}/{d}?
patterns.hint: The numerator tells how many parts to move from 0.
patterns.explanation: {k}/{d} is {k} {'part' if k == 1 else 'parts'} of 1/{d} from 0, so it is at mark number {k}.
patterns.misconception: Counts tick marks instead of intervals or starts the numerator count at one rather than zero.
patterns.notes: 3 to 15 equal parts.

patterns.text: A number line from 0 to {w} {'is divided into' if w == 1 else 'has each whole divided into'} {d} equal parts. How many tick marks does it have, counting the marks at both ends?
patterns.hint: Draw a small line with 2 equal parts and count its marks.
patterns.explanation: There are {w} × {d} = {w * d} equal parts. A line with {w * d} parts has one more mark than parts: {w * d} + 1 = {w * d + 1} marks.
patterns.misconception: Counts tick marks instead of intervals or starts the numerator count at one rather than zero.
patterns.notes: Lines from 0 to 1, 2 or 3 with 2 to 12 parts in each whole (33 different questions).

patterns.text: A number line from 0 to 2 is divided so that each whole has {d} equal parts. Counting the marks after 0, which mark number shows {n}/{d}?

steps.text: Sees that each part is 1/{d}, so 1 is at mark {d}.
Counts on {r} more {'part' if r == 1 else 'parts'}: {d} + {r} = mark {n} shows {n}/{d}.

patterns.hint: 1 whole is at mark {d}. {n}/{d} is more than 1.
patterns.explanation: Each part is 1/{d}. 1 = {d}/{d} is at mark {d}, and {n}/{d} is {r} {'part' if r == 1 else 'parts'} further: mark {n}.
patterns.misconception: Counts tick marks instead of intervals or starts the numerator count at one rather than zero.
patterns.notes: Each whole split into 2 to 10 parts; the fraction is between 1 and 2.

patterns.hint: Double the numerator and compare it with the denominator.
patterns.explanation: 2 × {n} = {2 * n}, which is {'less than' if 2 * n < d else ('equal to' if 2 * n == d else 'greater than')} {d}. So {n}/{d} is {'less than' if 2 * n < d else ('equal to' if 2 * n == d else 'greater than')} one-half.
patterns.misconception: Checks only whether the numerator itself is large without relating it to the denominator.

patterns.text: What numerator makes ___/{2 * m} exactly equal to one-half?
patterns.hint: Half of the denominator.

patterns.text: {who.name} has finished {n}/{d} {act}. Has {who.name} finished more than half?

doesn't compare twice the numerator with the denominator
doesn't use one-half as a benchmark

patterns.hint: Half of {d} is {d / 2:mixed}. Is {n} more or less than that?
patterns.explanation: Half of {d} is {d / 2:mixed}. {n} is {'more' if 2 * n > d else 'less'} than that, so {who.name} has finished {'more' if 2 * n > d else 'less'} than half.
patterns.misconception: Checks only whether the numerator itself is large without relating it to the denominator.
patterns.notes: Denominators 5 to 20; numerators of 3 or more (so a large-looking numerator can still be less than half); never exactly half.

patterns.text: A strip is divided into {2 * m} equal parts, and {n} {'part is' if n == 1 else 'parts are'} coloured. How many more parts must be coloured so that exactly one-half of the strip is coloured?

steps.text: Finds one-half of the strip: {2 * m} ÷ 2 = {m} parts.
Finds the extra parts: {m} − {n} = {m - n}.

patterns.hint: How many parts make one-half of {2 * m} parts?
patterns.explanation: One-half of {2 * m} parts is {m} parts. {n} are coloured, so {m} − {n} = {m - n} more are needed.
patterns.misconception: Checks only whether the numerator itself is large without relating it to the denominator.
patterns.notes: Strips of 6 to 24 equal parts (even); fewer than half are coloured to start.

patterns.text: Choose the correct symbol: {a}/{b} ___ {c}/{d}.

wrong.mistake: compares the numerators or the denominators on their own
thinks the fractions are equal because they share a number
thinks the fractions can't be compared without a picture

patterns.hint: Write both fractions with the same denominator, {lcm(b, d)}.
patterns.explanation: {a}/{b} = {a * lcm(b, d) // b}/{lcm(b, d)} and {c}/{d} = {c * lcm(b, d) // d}/{lcm(b, d)}. So {a}/{b} {'<' if f < g else '>'} {c}/{d}.
patterns.misconception: Compares numerators or denominators separately without creating a common basis.
patterns.notes: Two proper fractions in simplest form with different numerators and denominators 2 to 12.

patterns.text: Which fraction is the greatest?

wrong.mistake: picks the fraction with the largest numerator
picks the fraction with a larger denominator
compares without a common denominator or a benchmark

steps.text: Uses a common denominator, a benchmark (1/2, 1) or cross-multiplying to compare the fractions.
Chooses {f.r} as the greatest.

patterns.hint: Compare each fraction with one-half, or rewrite them with the same denominator.
patterns.explanation: Comparing with equivalent fractions (or by cross-multiplying), {f.r} is the greatest. {f.w1} has a bigger numerator but a smaller value.
patterns.misconception: Compares numerators or denominators separately without creating a common basis.
patterns.notes: 150 sets of four proper fractions in simplest form (listed in the pattern), denominators up to 20. In 50 the greatest is below one-half; in many others two or more options are above one-half. The greatest is at least 1/10 more than each of the others (no near ties). One wrong option has a bigger numerator and one a bigger denominator than the right answer.

patterns.text: {p.name} {what.do} {a}/{b} {what.u} and {q.name} {what.do} {c}/{d} {what.u}. Who {what.do} farther?

wrong.mistake: compares the numerators or the denominators on their own

patterns.misconception: Compares numerators or denominators separately without creating a common basis.
patterns.notes: Two proper fractions with denominators 2 to 10, different numerators and denominators.

patterns.text: {who.name} had {t} {g.many} and used {a}/{b} of them. How many {g.many} are left?
patterns.hint: Find the number used first, then subtract it from {t}.

patterns.misconception: Applies a remembered rule without checking the whole, equality of parts or the meaning of the answer.
patterns.notes: Denominators 2 to 10; totals are a multiple of the denominator, up to 150.

patterns.text: A class has {t} counters. Group A uses {a}/{b} of them and Group B uses {c}/{d} of them. How many more counters does the larger share have?
patterns.answer: abs(t * a // b - t * c // d)
patterns.hint: Find each group's counters first, then subtract.
patterns.explanation: Group A: {a}/{b} of {t} = {t * a // b}. Group B: {c}/{d} of {t} = {t * c // d}. The difference is {abs(t * a // b - t * c // d)}.
patterns.misconception: Applies a remembered rule without checking the whole, equality of parts or the meaning of the answer.
patterns.notes: Two different fractions (denominators 2 to 12) of the same 12 to 120 counters, together at most the whole.

patterns.text: Team A gets {a}/{b} of {t1} {g.many}. Team B gets {c}/{d} of {t2} {g.many}. Which team gets more {g.many}?

wrong.expr: 'Team B' if s1 > s2 else 'Team A'
wrong.mistake: compares the fractions without checking that the wholes are different
doesn't work out the actual amounts
doesn't find a fraction of each quantity

steps.text: Finds both amounts: {a}/{b} of {t1} = {s1} and {c}/{d} of {t2} = {s2}.
Concludes {'Team A' if s1 > s2 else 'Team B'} gets more ({max(s1, s2)} > {min(s1, s2)}).

patterns.hint: The wholes are different, so find each team's actual number.
patterns.explanation: Team A: {t1} ÷ {b} × {a} = {s1}. Team B: {t2} ÷ {d} × {c} = {s2}. {'Team A' if s1 > s2 else 'Team B'} gets more{', even though its fraction is the smaller one' if trap == 1 else ''}.
patterns.misconception: Applies a remembered rule without checking the whole, equality of parts or the meaning of the answer.
patterns.notes: Denominators 2 to 6; different wholes (multiples of the denominators). In two copies of three, the team with the larger fraction gets FEWER (the trap); in the rest it gets more, so the fractions alone never decide.

patterns.text: {who.name} had ₹{t:num}. {who.name} spent {a}/{b} of it on books, and then {c}/{d} of the money left on a bag. How much money does {who.name} have now?

steps.text: Books: {a}/{b} of ₹{t:num} = ₹{spent1}; money left = ₹{rest}.
Bag: {c}/{d} of ₹{rest} = ₹{spent2}; money now = ₹{rest - spent2}.

patterns.hint: The second fraction is of the money LEFT, not of ₹{t:num}.
patterns.explanation: Books: ₹{t:num} ÷ {b} × {a} = ₹{spent1}, leaving ₹{rest}. Bag: ₹{rest} ÷ {d} × {c} = ₹{spent2}. Money now: ₹{rest} − ₹{spent2} = ₹{rest - spent2}.
patterns.misconception: Applies a remembered rule without checking the whole, equality of parts or the meaning of the answer.
patterns.notes: Denominators 2 to 5; amounts in tens up to ₹2,000, chosen so every step is whole rupees.

patterns.text: A school has {t} students. {a}/{b} of them come by bus. {c}/{d} of the rest walk to school, and the others come by cycle. How many students come by cycle? Show your working.
patterns.answer: By bus: {t} ÷ {b} × {a} = {bus}. The rest: {t} − {bus} = {rest}. Walk: {rest} ÷ {d} × {c} = {walk}. By cycle: {rest} − {walk} = {cyc}.

steps.text: By bus: {a}/{b} of {t} = {bus}, so {rest} are left.
Walk: {c}/{d} of the {rest} left = {walk} (not {c}/{d} of {t}).
By cycle: {rest} − {walk} = {cyc} students.

patterns.hint: The second fraction is of the students left, not of the whole school.
patterns.explanation: {bus} come by bus, leaving {rest}. {walk} of those walk, so {cyc} come by cycle.
patterns.misconception: Applies a remembered rule without checking the whole, equality of parts or the meaning of the answer.
patterns.notes: 40 to 400 students; denominators 2 to 5; every step is a whole number of students.

patterns.text: Compare {a}/{b} and {c}/{d} by writing them as equivalent fractions with the same denominator. Which is greater, and by how much? Show your working.
patterns.answer: A common denominator is {l}. {a}/{b} = {x}/{l} and {c}/{d} = {y}/{l}. {max(x, y)}/{l} > {min(x, y)}/{l}, so {a if x > y else c}/{b if x > y else d} is greater, by {max(x, y) - min(x, y)}/{l}.

steps.text: Chooses a common denominator such as {l} (any common multiple is fine).
Writes {a}/{b} = {x}/{l} and {c}/{d} = {y}/{l}, and says {a if x > y else c}/{b if x > y else d} is greater.
Difference: {max(x, y) - min(x, y)}/{l} (or the same amount in another form, e.g. simplified).

patterns.hint: Find a number that both {b} and {d} divide into.
patterns.explanation: With denominator {l}: {x}/{l} and {y}/{l}. The difference is {max(x, y) - min(x, y)}/{l}.
patterns.misconception: Compares numerators or denominators separately without creating a common basis.
patterns.notes: Two proper fractions in simplest form, denominators 2 to 9 where neither divides the other; common denominator up to 40.

patterns.text: Each {item} is cut into {d} equal pieces. {who.name} has {n} pieces. (a) Write the amount as an improper fraction of a {item}. (b) Write it as a mixed number. (c) How many more pieces would {who.name} need to have {w + 1} whole {item}s? Show your working.
patterns.answer: (a) {n}/{d}. (b) {n} ÷ {d} = {w} remainder {r}, so {w} {r}/{d}. (c) {w + 1} wholes = {(w + 1) * d} pieces, so {(w + 1) * d} − {n} = {d - r} more {'piece' if d - r == 1 else 'pieces'}.

steps.text: (b) {w} {r}/{d} (the remainder {r} stays over {d}).
(c) {(w + 1) * d} − {n} = {d - r} more {'piece' if d - r == 1 else 'pieces'}.

patterns.hint: Each whole {item} is {d} pieces.
patterns.explanation: {n} pieces of 1/{d} is {n}/{d} = {w} {r}/{d}. {w + 1} wholes need {(w + 1) * d} pieces, so {d - r} more.
patterns.misconception: Uses the remainder as a whole-number part or changes the denominator during conversion.
patterns.notes: 3 to 8 pieces in each whole; 1 to 4 wholes and some left over.

patterns.text: {who.name} has ₹{t:num}. {who.name} spends {a}/{b} of it on a storybook and {c}/{d} of it on stationery. (a) How much does the storybook cost? (b) How much does the stationery cost? (c) How much is spent in all? (d) What fraction of the money is left? (e) How much money is left? Show your working.
patterns.answer: (a) ₹{t:num} ÷ {b} × {a} = ₹{book}. (b) ₹{t:num} ÷ {d} × {c} = ₹{stat}. (c) ₹{book} + ₹{stat} = ₹{spent}. (d) {left}/{t} = {frac(left, t):fraction} of the money is left. (e) ₹{t:num} − ₹{spent} = ₹{left}.

steps.text: (a) {a}/{b} of ₹{t:num} = ₹{book}.
(b) {c}/{d} of ₹{t:num} = ₹{stat}.
(c) ₹{book} + ₹{stat} = ₹{spent}.
(d) {frac(left, t):fraction} (accept {left}/{t} or any equivalent fraction, e.g. 1 − {a}/{b} − {c}/{d} worked with a common denominator).
(e) ₹{left} (follow through from a wrong (c)).

patterns.hint: Both fractions are of the same ₹{t:num}.
patterns.explanation: Storybook ₹{book}, stationery ₹{stat}, spent ₹{spent}, left ₹{left}, which is {frac(left, t):fraction} of ₹{t:num}.
patterns.misconception: Applies a remembered rule without checking the whole, equality of parts or the meaning of the answer.
patterns.notes: Amounts from ₹100 to ₹2,000 that both denominators divide; the two fractions together are less than the whole.

patterns.text: Three equal {item}s are shared. {p.name} eats {a}/{trio.b} of one, {q.name} eats {c}/{trio.d} of another and {r.name} eats {e}/{trio.f} of the third. (a) Write all three fractions with the same denominator. (b) Put the three amounts in order from least to greatest. (c) Who ate the most? (d) How much more did that child eat than the child who ate the least? Show your working.
patterns.answer: (a) Common denominator {l}: {a}/{trio.b} = {x}/{l}, {c}/{trio.d} = {y}/{l}, {e}/{trio.f} = {z}/{l}. (b) In order: {bot}/{l}, {x + y + z - top - bot}/{l}, {top}/{l}. (c) {p.name if top == x else (q.name if top == y else r.name)} ate the most. (d) {top}/{l} − {bot}/{l} = {top - bot}/{l} of a {item} more.

steps.text: (a) 1 mark for a common denominator such as {l}; 1 mark for all three: {x}/{l}, {y}/{l}, {z}/{l}.
(b) {bot}/{l}, {x + y + z - top - bot}/{l}, {top}/{l} (or the original fractions in that order).
(c) {p.name if top == x else (q.name if top == y else r.name)}.
(d) {top - bot}/{l} of a {item} (accept an equivalent fraction).

patterns.hint: Find a number that {trio.b}, {trio.d} and {trio.f} all divide into.
patterns.explanation: With denominator {l} the amounts are {x}/{l}, {y}/{l} and {z}/{l}; the most is {top}/{l} and the least {bot}/{l}.
patterns.misconception: Compares numerators or denominators separately without creating a common basis.
patterns.notes: Ten sets of three denominators (2 to 15) with a common denominator up to 60; three different amounts; three different children.

patterns.text: A school garden has {t} plants. {a}/{b} of them are roses and {c}/{d} of them are marigolds. The rest are tulsi plants. (a) How many roses are there? (b) How many marigolds? (c) How many tulsi plants? (d) What fraction of the plants are tulsi, in simplest form? (e) Are the tulsi plants more or less than half of the garden? Explain. Show your working.
patterns.answer: (a) {t} ÷ {b} × {a} = {ro} roses. (b) {t} ÷ {d} × {c} = {ma} marigolds. (c) {t} − {ro} − {ma} = {tu} tulsi plants. (d) {tu}/{t} = {frac(tu, t):fraction}. (e) Half of {t} is {t // 2}; {tu} is {'more' if 2 * tu > t else 'less'} than {t // 2}, so the tulsi plants are {'more' if 2 * tu > t else 'less'} than half.

steps.text: (a) {a}/{b} of {t} = {ro} roses.
(b) {c}/{d} of {t} = {ma} marigolds.
(c) {t} − {ro} − {ma} = {tu} tulsi plants (follow through).
(d) {frac(tu, t):fraction} (from {tu}/{t}).
(e) Compares {tu} with half of {t} ({t // 2}): {'more' if 2 * tu > t else 'less'} than half, with the reason.

patterns.hint: Find each kind of plant from the whole {t}; the rest are tulsi.
patterns.explanation: {ro} roses + {ma} marigolds leaves {tu} tulsi plants, which is {frac(tu, t):fraction} of the garden.
patterns.misconception: Multiplies by the denominator instead of dividing the whole into equal groups first.
patterns.notes: 24 to 240 plants (an even number that both denominators divide); never exactly half tulsi.

patterns.stimulus: Case study: A 1 km walking track in a park has markers that split it into {d} equal parts, like a number line from 0 km to 1 km. {who.name} starts at 0 and stops at marker number {k}, counting the markers after 0.

parts.text: (a) What fraction of a kilometre has {who.name} walked? Write it as a/b.

parts.text: (b) What fraction of the track is still left to walk? Write it as a/b.
(c) There is also a marker at 0 km and one at 1 km. How many markers are there in all?
parts.explanation: {d} parts need {d - 1} markers in between, plus the two at the ends: {d + 1}.

parts.text: (d) A friend is at marker number {m}, counting the markers after 0. Is the friend more or less than halfway along the track?

options.correct: 'More than halfway' if 2 * m > d else 'Less than halfway'

wrong.expr: 'Less than halfway' if 2 * m > d else 'More than halfway'
wrong.mistake: doesn't compare the marker with half the parts
doesn't compare the marker with half the parts
confuses a marker number with the total number of parts

parts.explanation: Halfway is marker {d / 2:mixed}; marker {m} is {'more' if 2 * m > d else 'less'} than halfway.

patterns.misconception: Counts tick marks instead of intervals or starts the numerator count at one rather than zero.
patterns.notes: Tracks split into 4, 5, 6, 8 or 10 equal parts; the friend is never exactly halfway.

patterns.stimulus: Case study: {p.name} and {q.name} each bring a tiffin box with one same-sized paratha. At lunch {p.name} eats {a}/{pair.b} of {p.his} paratha and {q.name} eats {c}/{pair.l} of {q.his} paratha.

options.correct: p.name if x > c else q.name

wrong.expr: q.name if x > c else p.name
wrong.mistake: compares numerators or denominators on their own
doesn't use the common denominator
thinks different denominators can't be compared

parts.explanation: {max(x, c)}/{pair.l} > {min(x, c)}/{pair.l}, so {p.name if x > c else q.name} ate more.

parts.text: (c) How much more paratha did that child eat? Write it in simplest form.
(d) If the two eaten pieces were put together, what fraction of one paratha would they make? Write it in simplest form.

patterns.misconception: Compares numerators or denominators separately without creating a common basis.
patterns.notes: Related denominators only (one is a multiple of the other: 2 and 4, 3 and 9, 4 and 12 and so on); different amounts; the two pieces together are less than one paratha.
